Question 1

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), where F(x,y)=(12x3−1y)i+(x−1y2)j.

a
f(x,y)=12x4+x2y−xy+C
b
f(x,y)=3x4−1y+C
c
f(x,y)=12x3y−xy+C
d
f(x,y)=12x3−1y+C
e
f(x,y)=3x4−xy+1y+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating f_x=12x^3-1/y with respect to x gives f=3x^4-x/y+g(y). Then f_y=x/y^2+g'(y)=(x-1)/y^2, so g'(y)=-1/y^2 and g(y)=1/y+C. Thus option e has the required gradient for y≠0.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ g(y) & =\frac{1}{y}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=\frac{1}{y}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+\frac{1}{y}+C.
$$

Question 1
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), where F(x,y)=(12x3−1y)i+(x−1y2)j.

a
f(x,y)=12x4+x2y−xy+C
b
f(x,y)=3x4−1y+C
c
f(x,y)=12x3y−xy+C
d
f(x,y)=12x3−1y+C
e
f(x,y)=3x4−xy+1y+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=12x3−1y,∂f∂y=x−1y2

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(12x3−1y)dx=3x4−xy+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain

∂f∂y=xy2+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=x−1y2 into account, we obtain xy2+g′(y)=x−1y2xy2+g′(y)=xy2−1y2g′(y)=−1y2g(y)=1y+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=1y+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=3x4−xy+1y+C.

content.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Two-Variable Function From Its Gradient
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ g(y) & =\frac{1}{y}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=\frac{1}{y}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+\frac{1}{y}+C.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+x{e}^{xy}\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(z) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z) \\ h(z) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
content.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+x{e}^{xy}\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(z) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z) \\ h(z) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C.
$$

Question 3
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), where F(x,y)=yexy i+(xexy+2y) j.

a
f(x,y)=xexy+2+C
b
f(x,y)=yexy+x2+C
c
f(x,y)=exy+y2+C
d
f(x,y)=exy+xy+C
e
f(x,y)=xyexy+y+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating f_x=ye^{xy} with respect to x gives f=e^{xy}+g(y). Then f_y=xe^{xy}+g'(y), so g'(y)=2y and g(y)=y^2+C. Option c therefore has exactly the required gradient.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{xy}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{xy}+{y}^{2}+C.
$$

Question 3
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), where F(x,y)=yexy i+(xexy+2y) j.

a
f(x,y)=xexy+2+C
b
f(x,y)=yexy+x2+C
c
f(x,y)=exy+y2+C
d
f(x,y)=exy+xy+C
e
f(x,y)=xyexy+y+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=yexy,∂f∂y=xexy+2y

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫yexydx=exy+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain

∂f∂y=xexy+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=xexy+2y into account, we obtain xexy+g′(y)=xexy+2yg′(y)=2yg(y)=y2+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=y2+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=exy+y2+C.

content.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Two-Variable Function From Its Gradient
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{xy}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{xy}+{y}^{2}+C.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+(3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z})\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+C.
$$

EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=y2z3−ez,∂f∂y=2xyz3,∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(y2z3−ez)dx=xy2z3−xez+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=2xyz3+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=2xyz3 into account, we obtain 2xyz3+∂g∂y=2xyz3∂g∂y=0

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫0dy=h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=xy2z3−xez+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez into account, we obtain 3xy2z2−xez+h′(z)=3xy2z2−xezh′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

content.knowledge_point: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient
content.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+(3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z})\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+C.
$$

Question 5
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f=F, where F(x,y)=eyi+(xey+2y)j.

a
f(x,y)=x2ey+y+C
b
f(x,y)=2yey+x2+C
c
f(x,y)=xey+y+C
d
f(x,y)=xey+y2+C
e
f(x,y)=yey+xy2+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating f_x=e^y with respect to x gives f=xe^y+g(y). Then f_y=xe^y+g'(y), so g'(y)=2y and g(y)=y^2+C. Thus option d has the required gradient.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{e}^{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{y}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}+C.
$$

Question 5

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f=F, where F(x,y)=eyi+(xey+2y)j.

a
f(x,y)=x2ey+y+C
b
f(x,y)=2yey+x2+C
c
f(x,y)=xey+y+C
d
f(x,y)=xey+y2+C
e
f(x,y)=yey+xy2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=ey,∂f∂y=xey+2y

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫eydx=xey+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=xey+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=xey+2y into account, we obtain xey+g′(y)=xey+2yg′(y)=2yg(y)=y2+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=y2+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=xey+y2+C.

content.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{e}^{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{y}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}+C.
$$
